newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's latest constitutional change under fire.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's latest constitutional change under fire.

text.p: A constitutional amendment banning MPs from floor-crossing came under fire from some newspapers and commentators in Pakistan on Wednesday.
"It is against the spirit of democracy," former law minister and retired Supreme Court judge Fakhruddin Ebrahim told Reuters. "This law has ignored the basic values of the constitution."

Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif used his huge parliamentary majority to push the amendment unopposed through the Senate and National Assembly this week, the second time he has changed the constitution since sweeping to power in elections in February.
On both occasions the government failed to submit the bills to standing committees for debate before moving to a vote, effectively snuffing out any chance for prior public debate.

The mass-circulation Urdu-language newspaper Jang, while accepting the need to "purge the country's politics of the ills of horse-trading and switching loyalties for financial gain", criticised what it called the government's legislative haste.
It also argued that the latest amendment demanded over-rigid obedience to party discipline for dubious gains.

"In all the world's democracies, MPs are not supposed strictly to follow the party line in debates on important laws. If they have to follow the party line alone, there is no point in debating draft laws in parliament," the paper said.
"For all MPs, national interest should be supreme and above party interest. Honest opinion and dissent on principles... should not be considered as violation of party discipline."
The amendment means a parliamentarian may lose his seat if he breaches party discipline, votes against the party line or abstains from voting in defiance of party policy.
Once a party's disciplinary committee acts against an alleged defector, the MP concerned may appeal only to his party leader, whose decision overrides that of any court in the land.

"Notwithstanding anything contained in the constitution, no court, including the Supreme Court and a High Court, shall entertain any legal proceedings, exercise any jurisdiction or make any order in relation to any action under this Article (of the constitution)," the amendment says.
Ebrahim said this amounted to a denial of basic rights.

"This is a very serious matter," he said. "A man must have the right to go to a court of law...Each one of us is entitled to invoke fundamental rights. You (the government) are denying fundamental rights to the parliamentarians."
He poured scorn on the amendment's stipulation that MPs must follow party policy, saying this was impossible to define. "What is party policy, where it exists?" he asked.

Benazir Bhutto's opposition Pakistan People's Party supported the amendment, but Ebrahim said the consensus did not necessarily make the amendment right. First and foremost, a law should be "just, fair and reasonable", he argued.

The English-language daily The News said the constitutional amendment passed by the Sharif government in April, removing presidential powers to sack elected governments, had transferred power from the president to parliament.
"The 14th amendment (against floor-crossing) has delivered this (power) to party leaders -- posing a real danger of the legislature becoming a rubber stamp," the newspaper said.
